Retail technology innovation of the week: Uber Eats teams with Coco to bring robot delivery to EU
Retail Technology Innovation of the Week is a series brought to you by RTIH, highlighting stand out deployments, launches, and initiatives by retailers and tech suppliers. Every week, we showcase forward thinking tech plays that have impressed our Editor and the Retail Technology Innovations Report judging panel, building up to the publication of the 2026 report later this year.
And this week we’re focusing on Uber Eats which is bringing robot delivery to the EU. This week, Finland will become the first EU market where its customers can get their orders delivered by autonomous robots, starting in central Helsinki through a partnership with Coco Robotics. Customers matched with a robot can follow its journey in the Uber Eats app.
A spokesperson says: “We’re growing fast in Finland. We launched Uber Eats in May with three cities, and just three months later we’re adding eight more, bringing us to 11 cities and areas across the country. Helsinki is a particularly exciting place to take this next step: the robots have already been put through their paces on the city’s streets and in Finnish winter conditions. Now they’ll be delivering for Uber Eats alongside our existing courier network.”
And honourable mentions this week to...
Officeworks
Australian retailer Officeworks, part of the Wesfarmers group, has become the first retailer globally to activate Snapchat's suite of advertising formats directly within the Zitcha platform. This includes Sponsored Snaps, Snapchat's in-chat ad format that delivers full screen video or images directly into the Chat feed; Snap Ads (single image or video) to drive awareness, engagement, traffic and sales; and catalogue powered Dynamic Product Ads to blend storytelling with dynamic product discovery.
Officeworks kicked things off with a campaign for Microsoft to drive demand both online and in-store.
Andy Mossop, Chief Customer Officer at Officeworks, says: “We're focused on building a retail media network that creates value for everyone in the ecosystem, our customers, our suppliers and our business. That's why we're incredibly proud to partner with Zitcha and Snapchat to bring this innovative integration to life. As one of the first retailers globally to activate Snapchat through Zitcha, we're helping shape the future of retail media by connecting brands with audiences in more relevant and engaging ways.”
“Just as importantly, we're committed to delivering meaningful, measurable results for our suppliers. This work is a great example of what's possible when retailers, technology partners and brands come together with a shared focus on customer relevance and impact. We’re proud to provide a platform that delivers on this breadth of benefit to our supplier partners.”
Tesco
Last month we reported that Tesco was trialling Simbe’s Tally in-store shelf scanning robot.
Having kicked off with a single store, the pilot is now being extended to a small number of other locations. Thanks to Toby Pickard, Retail Futures Senior Partner at IGD, and a member of the judging panel for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, for bringing this to our attention.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: “I’ve now seen Simbe’s Tally robot in a third Tesco store in the UK - another store trialling autonomous inventory scanning. But this time, I had my son with me. His reaction was fascinating. He was completely intrigued by Tally: watching it move around the store, trying to work out what it was doing, and following it with the kind of curiosity only a child can bring to something that feels like it has just stepped out of the future.”
He added: “I’ve heard that in the US, some shoppers will even choose stores specifically because they have Tally, because their children love seeing the robot. Honestly, I can believe it. And it got me thinking…We often talk about retail automation in terms of efficiency, accuracy, labour productivity and ROI. But what happens when the technology itself becomes part of the customer experience? Could robots like Tally become something that customers - and especially children - actively want to see?”
Could, Pickard asked, the presence of robots change which stores people choose to visit? And perhaps more importantly: what happens when the next generation grows up thinking autonomous robots moving around a supermarket is completely normal? Will they see Tally as technology? Or simply as part of what a modern store is?
Pickard concluded: “There’s a fascinating intersection here between automation, operations, customer experience and the psychology of physical retail. I’m increasingly convinced that the question isn’t just, what can robots do for retailers? It’s also, what can robots make customers feel about the future of retail?”

items.summary: The billionaire owner of Frasers Group and former owner of Newcastle United football club hit out at what he called 'recent populist proposals.'
items.body:
Mike Ashley launches scathing attack on Burnham's 'delusional' plans to revive the high street
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Sports Direct tycoon Mike Ashley has launched a scathing attack on Andy Burnham's 'delusional' plans to revive the high street and has warned retailers will be 'further devastated' unless taxes are cut.
In a letter to the Prime Minister, the billionaire owner of Frasers Group and former owner of Newcastle United football club, Ashley hit out at what he called 'recent populist proposals.'
Burnham this week insisted he would 'take pressure off' businesses, which have complained about consumers having less cash to spend while their own operating costs have soared in recent years.
His plans include funding business rates discounts for pubs and clubs by increasing business rates on online retail warehouses as well as tougher rules for unseemly vape and betting shops.
But Ashley - whose stable of retailers encompasses House of Fraser, Flannels, Sofa.com, Jack Wills and Evans Cycles - said that it would be 'simply delusional' to tax larger retailers more through raising rates further.
Ashley said there were 'real' challenges facing the country's economy that needed to be tackled, rather than 'topics which provide good media soundbites.'
Letter to the Prime Minister: Mike Ashley has urged Andy Burnham to not just focus on 'topics which provide good media soundbites'
He lambasted a 'disastrous' approach to business rates and 'the dramatically increasing cost of employing people' as the biggest obstacles for businesses.
These factors - including Keir Starmer's government's increases to minimum wages and employer National Insurance contributions - have backfired and led to retailers cutting jobs, he said.
In a plea ahead of the Budget on 28 October, Ashley said: 'These aspects of the hostile business climate can't be allowed to continue or the high streets will be further devastated.'
Ashley mentioned his £40million rescue of troubled department store chain Harvey Nichols earlier this month. He asked Burnham: 'My challenge to you is - how are you going to help with turning Harvey Nichols around?'
What's more, he said a shop-lifting epidemic was 'getting much worse' in Britain and called for measures to help protect shops from theft.
Frasers loses around £40m per year from theft, he said, while incidents of theft also sometimes put staff at risk.
Ashley also took a swipe at Burnham's remarks around retailers offering misleading Recommended Retail Prices (RRPs) and phoney discounts.
He said that his Sports Direct brand often uses big discounts while it advertises 'up to 90 per cent off the RRP' to online shoppers. 'The driving down of prices through discounting is what helps the consumer by giving them better value and helps with their cost of living,' he said.
He said there was no inherent problem with RRPs, which are set by reputable companies, such as Nike, Adidas and Puma.
But he urged scrutiny of 'price fixing' in the sportswear market, 'where consumers will actually be paying too much because retailers can't discount as they want.' He said that prices for official England shirts were 'uncannily uniform at £134.99 across the board' during this summer's World Cup.
This price had been achieved by tactics that make the market 'less competitive,' he added.
Ashley said the competition watchdog handed out fines which 'have been disproportionately low and toothless and so the behaviours don't stop.'
He concluded: 'This is just one example of many - and this should be the focus of government in relation to the protection of consumers - looking at legal changes to prevent brands limiting distribution in order to support price fixing.'

Zara owner's new fast-fashion brand Lefties struts onto UK high street in major challenge to Primark
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Zara’s stylish little sister chain Lefties is sweeping into Britain, bringing a robot army to support its bid to win over value-conscious families refreshing their wardrobes and homes this autumn.
Lefties, the rapidly-expanding discount chain owned by Zara group Inditex, launched its first UK store this morning in Liverpool One, the city's top shopping complex.
Despite the rain, queues formed outside the glossy 27, 000 sq ft store, the first of three that will open this year. Lakeside in Essex and Metrocentre near Newcastle will follow.
Some people in the queue had travelled from Leeds eager to sample the Lefties' latest things-for-less formula.
Xavier Rus Riera, Lefties general director, declined to say how many stores Inditex planned to open in the UK: 'We don't have a number; we're trying to meet the requirements of customers. It's like football we will proceed match by match.'
Nevertheless, thanks to the help of robots that sort hangers at the tills and other automation, Lefties which already operates 225 stores in 20 markets worldwide, is set to pose a challenge to Primark.
Lefties opened its first UK store in a major challenge to Primark, using robots to cut costs
The retail division of Associated British Foods, which is set for a stock market float next year after a separation of the brands, is Britain’s most powerful high street player in affordable clothing and decor with about 190 stores.
But Lefties offer of low prices and glamorous store fit-outs will highlight the workaday feel of Primark outlets.
Automation will aid Lefties' drive for a share of hard-pressed households' budgets, too.
At the opening, a screen shows which dressing room is free, and unwanted items can put down a hatch in the dressing room to be sorted below.
At the self check-outs, hangers removed from garments are sorted by robot arms that add a sci-fi element to shopping. A light goes on at the check-out if anyone tries not to pay for something, too.
Lefties is also deploying technology to ensure that the displays are replenished.
In the stock room at Liverpool One, a system automatically separates newly-delivered items from one main rail into individual rails for each section. The Liverpool One store has created 150 locally recruited jobs but Lefties wants its staff on the shop floor, rather than engaged in less profitable activities.
The name of the chain derives not from left-wing politics but from Lefties' beginnings as a place where leftover Zara stock was sold.
Subsequently, the offer has evolved into 'total looks' of the latest in vogue items and also basics for women, teenagers, men and children, plus elegant homeware.
Studded jeans modelled by model Leomie Anderson have the designer vibe for £22.99.
Zara adopts each individual store's range to local preferences and, in line with this strategy, Lefties Liverpool is offering lots of leggings from £5.99 - and thermals from £9.99. It is Lefties's first foray into this cold-weather clothing introduced specially for the chilly months in the city.

items.title: Operation finds a third of Bristol independent stores selling illegal tobacco
items.summary: The latest test-purchasing operation commissioned by JTI UK found that a third (34%) of independent Bristol East shops selling tobacco visited sold illegal tobacco. Of those stores, seven directed undercover officers off-site to access illicit products, including two retailers who used cars parked outside their shops and one who supplied tobacco from a neighbouring flat. These alternative locations showcase the lengths illegal traders are going… This story continues at Operation finds a third of Bristol independent stores selling illegal tobacco Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Of those stores, seven directed undercover officers off-site to access illicit products, including two retailers who used cars parked outside their shops and one who supplied tobacco from a neighbouring flat.
These alternative locations showcase the lengths illegal traders are going to evade raids and avoid detection by enforcement agencies.
Previous test purchasing in the city had also found illegal tobacco products being sold in three of the complicit stores – suggesting that enforcement efforts need to be bolstered to stop repeat offenders.
Among the illegal products bought were Amber Leaf 50g ranging from £5.00 (counterfeit product) to £23.00 (non UK duty paid product), Platinum Tobacco (sourced from Zambia) for £4.50 and Marlboro for £5.00.
New polling commissioned by the It Costs More Than You Think campaign found that 97% of residents surveyed in Bristol are concerned by the consequence of illegal tobacco trade funding organised crime – but only 29% believe that the illegal tobacco trade is a serious issue that requires stricter enforcement, lower than the national average.
In addition, seven in ten residents surveyed in Bristol don’t believe it’s their responsibility to act on illegal tobacco, and 78% don’t think that their actions would make a difference when it comes to reducing illegal tobacco in their city.
Instead, three in four residents surveyed in Bristol believe politicians are not doing enough to prevent illegal tobacco trading.
“The lengths that criminals are taking to hide from the law – such as storing illegal products in cars or even different properties – shows that enforcement efforts need to be heavily bolstered to combat these rogue traders,” said Dale Stacey, communications manager at JTI UK. “Otherwise, illegal tobacco will continue to undermine honest businesses in Bristol and fuel organised crime in the community.
“The survey data also makes it clear that Bristolians don’t think it’s their responsibility to tackle this black market and are instead looking for more action from politicians.
“We are urgently calling for stronger penalties and more effective enforcement mechanisms to ensure these repeat offenders are held accountable.”
JTI is calling on the government to treat illegal tobacco as a serious economic and social issue with three simple asks; cancel the double taxation on tobacco; introduce a licensing scheme; and increase penalties to fund enforcement.
David Johnston, former detective and senior police officer of the Metropolitan Police Service, commented: “The test purchasing results from Bristol East indicate a shift in criminal tactics compared to other locations investigated as part of the It Costs More Than You Think Campaign.
“Not only are we seeing more stores keeping illegal products outside of their premises, with the aim of being more agile in the face of law enforcement; we’re also seeing them stock illicit products at higher price points, further driving profits for criminal organisations.

items.title: Bots and bargains: Zara owner launches cut-price Lefties in UK to rival Primark
items.summary: First robot-assisted outlet opens in Liverpool to take on Shein and supermarkets in clothing, shoes and homewares Business live – latest updates The owner of Zara is taking on Primark, Shein and the supermarkets with the launch of its cut-price chain Lefties in Britain, backed by an army of robots. The Spanish fashion brand opened its first UK store in Liverpool on Thursday, a few weeks after quietly launching its UK website. Continue reading...
items.body:
The owner of Zara is taking on Primark, Shein and the supermarkets with the launch of its cut-price chain Lefties in Britain, backed by an army of robots.
The Spanish fashion brand opened its first UK store in Liverpool on Thursday, a few weeks after quietly launching its UK website.
The store has embraced robotics to reduce staffing costs, with self-checkouts that scan a whole basket in one go and a clothes hanger sorter. Shoppers put their hangers in a slot as they pay and they are taken on a hidden conveyor belt to two robots behind a screen that sort them into boxes for different sizes.
The outlet at the Liverpool One city centre development also has fitting rooms equipped with a hatch through which unwanted items go to be sorted behind the scenes, again by robots.
The garment-sorting system splits clothes into rails for each department ready to be taken away to the shop floor or packed into the stockroom.
The Liverpool store is the first of three Lefties planned in the UK this year. The other two will be in the Lakeside shopping centre in Essex and the Metrocentre near Newcastle. More are expected next year.
Just before the official opening, as more than 100 customers queued up to be the first British shoppers, the chain’s general director said the group was “not thinking about a specific number” of UK stores and would look at how the first few went before taking next steps.
Xavier Ruz Riera said Liverpool had been chosen as the first outlet as it was a city with a vibrant young population that as a port was “open to the world” and “has a great personality”.
The Lefties name comes from the fact its owner, Inditex, launched it in 1999 as an outlet for unsold, or leftover, items from Zara. However, it stopped selling its bigger sister brand’s clothing about a decade ago, instead stocking its own range of men’s, women’s and children’s clothing, shoes, and homewares from bedding to vases.
As Zara has moved slightly upmarket, Lefties has stepped in as a more cost-conscious option. Its products are a touch above Primark but below Shein on price, with dresses an average of £18, compared with £16 at the British chain and £18.50 at the Chinese-founded marketplace, according to analysis by the trade journal Retail Week.
In a nod to the UK’s winter weather, the Liverpool store is the first Lefties to stock thermal clothing, presenting a new competitor to Marks & Spencer and Uniqlo on basic underwear, with bras from £7.99.
Riera said the store would flex to meet local demands, taking feedback from its sales figures and shop staff.
Its clothing and stores have more focus on design than Primark and it offers a nationwide online delivery service, unlike its British rival which only offers click and collect from its website. However, Lefties does not offer frequent discounts in the same way as Shein or other rivals such as Tesco’s F&F or Matalan.
Its garment-sorting machine is also in use at five UK Zaras, but the clothes hanger sorting system is a first for the group in Britain.
The chain operates in 20 countries including Italy, Turkey and Romania, with 225 stores globally. The brand, now Inditex’s fastest-expanding chain, opened its first French and Italian stores last year and is set to go into Germany in the spring.
Riera said: “The UK is a natural next step offering an exciting destination for our brand. We believe there is a strong opportunity to bring our proposition to UK customers, offering quality fashion and home collections for the whole family at accessible prices through a seamless in-store and online shopping experience.”
Lefties’ online store offers its full collection, with free delivery on orders over £49 and the ability to order or return items for free in store.
It is likely to add to pressure on cheaper clothing chains such as Primark, New Look and Matalan as well as online specialists including Asos, Shein and Boohoo. However, it faces a market crowded with competitors, including successful supermarket own labels such as Tesco’s F&F, George at Asda and Sainsbury’s Tu.
Lefties’ parent group’s decision to prioritise other markets over the UK is likely to reflect apprehension about the level of competition itcould face here.
Richard Lim, the chief executive of the industry analyst Retail Economics, said: “Lefties’ arrival in the UK reflects successive waves of disruption across the apparel market. Competition has intensified from Chinese commerce players such as Shein, while the huge momentum behind pre-loved platforms such as Vinted has further fragmented consumer spending.”
He added: “This is a direct challenge to Primark’s heartland. Lefties gives Inditex a stronger foothold in value fashion as the fight for the value-conscious fashion shopper is only getting more intense.”

Halfords shares hit a four-year high this morning as warm weather helped to boost the retailer’s profit outlook for the year.
The bicycle and car parts chain said the ‘heightened seasonal demand’ for its products, including air conditioning, had delivered an extra £5million in profits.
An unusually warm summer has driven demand, with annual results now expected to be weighted to the first half, it said.

It offers a much-needed boost to Halfords, which is looking to ramp up sales and offset rising costs across its garage and retail arms.
Halfords said it planned to modernise its garage network by bringing specialist electric vehicle servicing equipment into most sites and giving staff tablets to support vehicle inspections.

The FTSE 250 firm returned to profit in its previous financial year after sales jumped 4.8 per cent on a like-for-like basis.
It said its repair services continued to gain traction in the period, as the firm believes Britain's ageing car stock presents an opportunity for growth.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG said: ‘Halfords shares have really climbed in recent months, and today's numbers seem to confirm that this wasn't just due to over-inflated expectations.

items.title: Retail sales melt away hitting jobs and investment - as survey reveals it's too hot to shop if temperatures top 25C
items.summary: Shoppers have been shunning Britain's sweltering high streets according to new industry figures to show evidence of weak consumer demand.
items.body:
Retail sales melt away hitting jobs and investment - as survey reveals it's too hot to shop if temperatures top 25C
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Shoppers have been shunning Britain’s sweltering high streets according to new industry figures to show evidence of weak consumer demand.
Retail volumes fell ‘at a steep pace’ in the year to August, monthly data from the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) showed.
It came as a separate survey from Barclays suggested it has been too hot to shop for much of the summer, with consumers unwilling to go out and spend once the temperature tops 25C.
The findings suggest that the heatwave has piled even more pressure on the high street, at a time when it is already being crushed with higher employer national insurance bills and minimum wages as well as Labour’s botched business rates reform.
The CBI said a balance of retail sales volumes, subtracting firms who saw sales fall from those who saw growth – fell to minus 48 per cent, down from minus 26 per cent in July.
Retailers have suffered in the heatwave as shoppers deem it too hot to shop
Sentiment about the wider business environment also took a tumble, declining to minus 29 per cent in August from -15 per cent the last time it was recorded in May.
The darkening mood means retailers are continuing to cut investment and jobs.
CBI lead economist Martin Sartorius said: ‘Retail firms grew more downbeat in August as they grappled with sharply falling sales volumes.’
Sartorius said as MPs return to Parliament this autumn the government must consider the steps needed to restore confidence in the sector.
He added: ‘Meaningful business rates reform is long overdue, with firms desperate for a fairer system that rewards – rather than penalises – investment and growth.
‘The Government should also look to cut employer NICs to support hiring and ensure the sector can continue to provide job opportunities, particularly for young people.’
Apart from facing steeply rising costs, retailers may be on the sharp end of falling consumer demand as the cost of living rises.
Yesterday, the energy regulator Ofgem revealed tariffs are on course to rise to a three-year representing a typical £60, or 4 per cent, added to annual bills, taking them to £1,723, as the Iran war pushes up the price of gas.
Experts at consultancy Cornwall Insight, a consultancy, expect an even steeper rise of 9pc to £1,872 in January, adding to pressure on households this winter.
At the same time, unemployment looks set to rise, with forecasts predicting it to climb past 5pc this year. The prospect of rising joblessness is weighing on consumer confidence according to a recent survey by S&P Global.
And the extended heatwave, with temperatures often reaching 30C over recent weeks, may also have proved unhelpful.
A survey from Barclays showed that on average UK adults believe 25.1C would be the limit representing when it is too hot to go shopping. The weather has benefited some retailers however, with garden centre and cool summer clothing benefiting.
Meanwhile, firms are prioritising investment in keeping cool, including air conditioning and ventilation, the report found.
Unsurprisingly perhaps, Barclays also revealed that air conditioning suppliers are in the money, with cash inflows up 4.3 per cent compared to the same month last year.
Official figures have painted a mixed picture of the summer so far for the high street.
Retail sales rose 0.7 per cent in June, boosted by demand for cool clothing and barbecues as well as air conditions but fell 0.5 per cent in July as shoppers had already bought what they needed to survive the heat, according to the Office for National Statistics.

items.title: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis
items.summary: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme . He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months. Continue reading...
items.body:
Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme.
He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months.
Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting.
“It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.”
A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years.
But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated.
“I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people. The last thing we want to see is a diagnosis of problems leading to a life on benefits.”
At a roundtable discussion, McFadden asked each of the young people how they felt as a result of their move into paid work. They cited better social lives and clearer daily routines.
“I’m so conscious, having done this job for almost exactly a year now, that belief and confidence is a big part of the picture,” McFadden told journalists afterwards. “We mustn’t blame young people for the challenges they are facing in the labour market.”
The number of Neets in the UK recently topped 1 million – with the latest data due out on Thursday.
Alan Milburn, the Blair-era cabinet minister reviewing youth inactivity for the government, has warned that the number could hit 1.25m by 2030, without intervention. His final report is due in the autumn.
McFadden made clear that welfare reform would probably be part of the government’s response, criticising the “black and white” distinction in the current universal credit system.
“There’s a design flaw in the universal credit system, which too readily separates people into ‘fit for work’ and ‘unfit for work’, and when they are unfit for work, leaves them without any support or any conditions,” he said. “That’s what I call the culture of ‘signed off and written off’. I think we need to change that.”
He highlighted a recent initiative under which claimants with no obligation to look for work have been asked to attend voluntary interviews with work coaches at their local Jobcentre.
McFadden had started the day at a branch of Sainsbury’s in London, stacking shelves in the bread aisle, alongside the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan.
The trio were highlighting the fact that Sainsbury’s is offering 10,000 internships for young people.
McFadden praised Boots and Sainsbury’s, and encouraged other big employers to play their part in what he called the “national cause” of tackling youth unemployment.
Asked whether it was a good use of public money to be subsidising corporations to take on young people, he said: “I’m enthused when businesses like Boots or Sainsbury’s – or any business in the country – steps up and says: ‘I want to play my part here.’ And if there’s a bit of a financial incentive in it, that’s fine.”
The jobs guarantee scheme will eventually be available to 18- to 24-year-olds in Great Britain who have been claiming universal credit and seeking work for at least 18 months, with the aim of creating 90,000 subsidised placements over the next three years.
It is initially being piloted in six areas with high unemployment, including central and east Scotland, Birmingham and Solihull, and south-east and south-west Wales. The government intends it to be nationwide by November.

items.title: Plug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first time
items.summary: DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills? Plug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity. Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers. Continue reading...
items.body:
Plug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity.
Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers.
Argos will be the first to offer the DIY solar systems this week, helping people living in flats or rented homes without roof access to lower their bills by generating their own electricity.
The rival retailers Amazon, Currys, B&Q and Screwfix are also expected to stock their shelves with plug-in panels within the coming weeks at prices starting from about £400 to £500 depending on the capacity of the system.
The devices are already popular in Spain and Germany, where they are known as Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant) because they can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.
The solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid. Each solar system must be registered so Great Britain’s National Energy System Operator can gauge how the cumulative impact of these panels could cut the need for gas-fired power or imports.
In the UK the 800-watt solar systems due to go on sale will be about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar set-up, meaning they are unable to provide enough energy to power a home but they could save the average household up to £110 a year on their annual electricity bill.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Plug-in solar is a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away.”
Graham Biggart, the managing director for Argos, said: “By making this technology more accessible, we’re putting more power in the hands of our customers and helping them explore practical ways to manage energy use at home.”
The savings possible from each solar system will depend on how much solar power is generated, which could be affected by the orientation of each solar panel and the weather on any given day.
Savings will also depend on whether the household is able to use the electricity while it is being generated – perhaps by running washing machines or dishwashers during sunny spells – because plug-in batteries were not included in the new legislation allowing plug-in solar sales to begin.
Emily Seymour, the energy editor at the Which? consumer group, said: “These smaller systems will generate less electricity than conventional rooftop solar and won’t be suitable for every home. People may need planning permission or the consent of the building owner before going ahead, so it will be important to check your own circumstances before making a purchase.
“There are also important safety considerations, particularly around the suitability of older electrical systems, the safe mounting of panels and the potential for people to use products or equipment incorrectly.”
Joanna O’Loan, a manager at Energy Saving Trust, said: “While the savings will vary from home to home, plug-in solar panels will give more people greater control over their energy use and costs. As these products become more widely available, access to clear and reliable information is essential to help people make informed choices that are right for their home and budget.”

Sainsbury's will offer work experience to 10,000 young people from the age of 14 in a bid to tackle the youth unemployment crisis.
Candidates across England, Scotland and Wales, will get to go behind the scenes in its stores and meet staff from various departments such as tech, logistics and food.
They’ll see how fresh produce reaches shelves ‘from farm to fork,’ and get help with CVs, interviews and job applications.
Split into two age groups, the programmes will launch in October 2026. The first scheme, KickStarter Insights is for 16 to 24-year-olds, while KickStart Explore is for 14 to 18-year-olds.

Kickstart Explore is designed for school students and will offer ‘a blend of in-school learning and practical work experience.’
This will include a mix of in-school workshops, digital sessions and store visits, adding up to roughly 24 hours per student.
Students can't apply directly as the scheme is organised through their school.
The programme will target schools with higher levels of free school meal uptake and communities where young people face the biggest barriers to work.
Sainbury's says it will cover lunch and travel for those taking part.
Simon Roberts, Sainsbury’s chief executive, said: ‘Few things matter more to us at Sainsbury’s than helping young people get on that first rung on the career ladder. With a quarter of our colleagues under 25, we see every day how much a first job can change lives.’
Young people face tough employment market
It comes as findings from the Work Foundation, a think-tank based at Lancaster University, report a tough employment outlook for young adults.
The report revealed 36 per cent of firms have reduced the number of entry-level jobs open to 16 to 24-year-olds in the past year.
And 73 per cent of bosses believe the rise in worklessness among young people is a ‘national crisis’.
Over one million young people aged 16 to 24 are classed as Neets – meaning they are not in employment, education or training.
Apprenticeships can be a brilliant gateway into certain careers, with the added bonus of not leaving those who get on to them saddled with debt.

items.title: ‘They make life much easier’: AI-powered shopping trolleys go on trial in Lancashire
items.summary: Customers give their verdicts as a Morrisons store becomes first in UK to test trolleys that scan, weigh and tally costs Lancashire has been the site of many British innovations throughout history, from the spinning jenny, which transformed textile production, to the creation of jelly babies. Now it has welcomed another first: AI shopping trolleys. Continue reading...
items.body:
Lancashire has been the site of many British innovations throughout history, from the spinning jenny, which transformed textile production, to the creation of jelly babies.
Now it has welcomed another first: AI shopping trolleys.
A Morrisons in Lancashire has become the first supermarket in the UK to trial the use of “smart trolleys” that allow customers to do their shopping without having to scan a single item.
The AI-powered Caper smart trolleys, created by San Francisco-based Instacart, automatically register each item placed in the trolley, adding up the cost and recommending related products as you shop. Once finished, customers can scan their trolley screen rather than visiting a checkout.
Preston is the first city in Britain to use them after the supermarket chain announced a deal to trial them at its location in Ashton-on-Ribble, to the west of the city.
Amazon Fresh, which allowed shoppers to take items from the shelves and leave the shop without checking out, using cameras to charge directly to online accounts, failed to take off in the UK, with the company’s last physical British store closing in 2025. But Morrisons is more hopeful that its smart trolleys will be a success, with plans to put them in supermarkets across the country.
The smart trolleys are already used in more than 100 cities across the world. They are similar in design and function to the Dash Cart used by Amazon’s former Fresh stores.
After the trolleys rolled into Ashton-on-Ribble last month, customer Matthew Byrne said they had “massively” helped him keep track of his shopping. Byrne is autistic and struggles to stick to set plans for what to get from the shops.
“Having what I’ve bought on screen has been great. I have a habit of just grabbing things and throwing them in my trolley, and then wondering how I’m paying so much. It’s been amazing to visualise it and see it in real time. I came here with an £80 budget, and I’ve actually been able to stick to it.”
Kaz Bond was disappointed to be forced to use a normal trolley for her latest shop due to a fault on her phone, having used them for every trip she has made to Morrisons since they became commonplace around four weeks ago.
“Honestly, I think they’re brilliant,” said Bond. “They make life much easier. I wouldn’t be that surprised if they’re everywhere before long. I reckon it’s the future.”
Debbie Files had chosen Tuesday as the day to take a leap of faith and use the trolleys for the first time, albeit with the help of a Morrisons employee.
“It was a little bit confusing at first, but you get used to it pretty quickly,” said Files. “It’s heavy, though. I’ve barely been able to turn it. I feel like I need a driving lesson to use it, but I got the hang of it. If they make a smaller one then that will get me to use it again.”

items.title: M&S amps up European ambitions with new online retail deal
items.summary: The British High Street retailer said it is working with the German company's logistics division Zeos to supply all its online customers across 22 markets in continental Europe.
items.body:
M&S amps up European ambitions with new online retail deal
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Marks & Spencer has stepped up its partnership with online retailer Zalando to help it fulfil customer orders in Europe.
The British High Street retailer said it is working with the German company’s logistics division Zeos to supply all its online customers across 22 markets in continental Europe.
The partnership means it has cut its logistics costs by up to a half and seen customer demand in Poland increase by 22 per cent in its first week of using the new system.
After a successful turnaround under chief executive Stuart Machin and chairman Archie Norman, the retailer has convinced younger shoppers of its style credentials and boosted sales in its fashion, homeware and beauty division.
International growth: The fashion retailer is attempting to woo more customers abroad
The group has recovered after fashion sales were last year hit by a cyber attack that disabled online shopping for almost two months.
Now it is hoping to woo even more shoppers abroad, including in its largest online markets France, the Netherlands, Germany and Spain.
Mark Lemming, managing director of international at M&S, said: ‘We have a clear ambition to grow our International business by bringing the best of M&S to more customers around the world.
'As demand for our fashion products grows across Europe, it's vital that we offer a seamless online shopping experience that matches the quality of our product.’
The partnership means that delivery times have been cut and return times have reduced from up to 35 days to eight days, M&S said.
M&S hopes to boost fortunes abroad after international sales fell 7.2pc over the year to 28 March. The business said this was partially due to shipment delays to the Middle East after war broke out in February.

items.body:
Woolworths’ latest Disney “Ooshie” collectibles have not only captivated Australian children, they have led to a short-term slump in competitor Coles’ sales.
Thousands of shoppers switched supermarkets to collect the plastic figurines, trading them online and in classrooms. Some schools have banned the toys, which can be collected after a customer spends $30, and environmentalists have labelled them “future landfill”.
The latest rubber figurine promotion was scheduled to end on Tuesday, but strong customer interest meant Woolworths prematurely ran out of Ooshies a week ago.
Coles on Tuesday released its full-year results, showing it had grown supermarket sales and gained market share against Woolworths in the 12 months to June.
Growth continued into July but then slumped amid a “competitor’s collectables campaign”, Coles announced.
The Coles chief executive, Leah Weckert, said the moderation in sales was a “temporary impact” lasting nearly four weeks. It mostly affected bricks-and-mortar shops rather than online shopping.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Michael Toner said the impact of the Woolworths campaign could scare Coles investors.
Ooshies, designed to fit on to the top of pens or pencils, come in generic packaging. It is not clear what figure you have received until the pack is ripped open, mostly by keen children who then trade the Ooshies at home or school in an attempt to collect all 40 characters, from Disney, Marvel and Star Wars.
Schoolchildren also stage Ooshie battles where they flick the characters to try to knock down competitors’ figures.
Woolworths has hosted dedicated swap meets across the country in recent weeks to help customers complete their collections.
Adult customers have turned to online marketplaces to trade Ooshies. A dedicated Facebook Ooshie swap group added almost 2,500 members in the past week and now has more than 45,000 members.
The 2019 Ooshies craze culminated in two farmers destroying a rare lion Ooshie live on TV in a protest against online bullying after they tried to sell it. On Tuesday, one eBay listing for an “ultra rare” fuzzy-textured figurine of Bullseye, the Toy Story horse, was set to sell for at least $750. Others are listed for thousands of dollars.
‘Just future landfill’
Prof Gary Mortimer, a consumer behaviour expert at the Queensland University of Technology business school, said Ooshies could help children build social skills – similar to when youngsters traded marbles or Pokémon cards last century.
“That was a part of the social etiquette of learning how to compromise and how to share,” Mortimer said.
“They’re looking for a particular one to complete the set and then negotiating – ‘so I’ll give you two of these for one of those’ – so I do think there’s some social benefits.”
But some schools have moved to shut down trading.
Bellevue Park state school in Queensland posted on Facebook that it had banned Ooshies due to “distractions, conflict and unfair trading”.
“We need your support to make sure these items remain safe at home and are not bought to school where they can become lost, damaged or stolen,” it wrote in a Facebook post.
One Sydney after-school care centre said it was no longer allowing the toys because there had been “disputes around trading and ownership, and situations where children have become upset or distressed”.
The bans are a badge of honour for Alan Ngov, the chief commercial officer at Headstart International, the company that developed Ooshies.
“You know it was a good one when you get banned from the school yard! What an amazing campaign from the Woolworths, Disney and Headstart teams!” he wrote on LinkedIn.
Environmental groups are concerned about the volume of plastic that will eventually end up in landfill. Kirsten Junor, the chief executive of not-for-profit Reverse Garbage, said the carbon emissions used to make and transport Ooshies outweighed any benefit.
“It’s just future landfill,” she said in a video posted on social media earlier this month.
“Kids don’t need them. We don’t need them. The planet doesn’t need them. Stop making them. You don’t need to get a reward every time you go shopping for what you need.”
Woolworths has said Ooshie figures are made from “97% recycled thermoplastic rubber”. The company has offered dedicated collection bins in some stores to recycle the figures.
Nearly two-thirds of parents surveyed by polling company YouGov said they changed their shopping behaviour due to the Ooshies promotion, including shopping at Woolworths more often.
One in five adult Ooshies collectors planned to sell the products online, YouGov’s survey released this week found. Millennials were most keen on collecting them, while baby boomers were interested in passing them on to loved ones.
Weckert said on Tuesday that Coles planned to continue its own promotional collectible campaigns in the future.
Coles reported its net profit rose 1% to $1.09bn in the year to June. Its supermarkets increased their profit margin on earnings from 5.3% to 5.7%.

items.title: Business rates 'tinkering' is not enough say campaigners as they demand full-scale overhaul of hated levy
items.summary: Ministers have been warned that 'tinkering' with Britain's hated business rates system is not enough as the government launched a consultation on reform.
items.body:
Business rates 'tinkering' is not enough say campaigners as they demand full-scale overhaul of hated levy
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Ministers have been warned that ‘tinkering’ with Britain’s hated business rates system is not enough as the government launched a consultation on reform.
Firms want to see a complete overhaul of the system which some say, as currently operated, means hospitality firms are ‘punished for success’.
Many high street operators also want to see more of the business rates burden shifted onto warehouses operated by online retailers.
The consultation – to be led by veteran tax expert Jerry Schurder – will review the way pub and hotel business rates bills are calculated.
Schurder will report back to the Treasury by March 2027. His recommendations will then be introduced in 2029 – the next time commercial properties are valued and the amount of rates they pay is determined.
James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, has said the review will feed into a plan to ‘build a fairer system for the future’.
But business chiefs said Labour must ‘move beyond piecemeal relief’ and offer radical reforms – as well as helping the High Street with rising costs at the Budget.
Jonathan Lawson, chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs in England, told the BBC that the current methodology for pubs’ bills means they are ‘punished for success’.
That is because their rates go up when their turnover increases.
By contrast, big online giants operating from warehouses are not affected by revenue-based calculations.
Bricks and mortar firms want Labour to deliver on its election pledge for a major shake-up to level the playing field between their premises and online operators.
Ros Morgan, chair of the Real Rates Reform Alliance, a coalition of business organisations calling for rates reform, said the review is ‘narrowly focused on pubs and hotels when what is needed is full-scale reform of the system.’
She added: ‘We cannot keep tinkering with business rates one sector at a time.
‘Any lasting solution for pubs and hotels must be part of a wider overhaul... which would create a broader tax base by ensuring all firms, including online, pay their fair share.’
Jonny Haseldine, head of business environment policy at the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said full reform was ‘urgently needed’ and a ‘continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach.’
UK Hospitality chief executive Allen Simpson said the plans would not ‘solve the immediate financial challenges caused by rising business rates bills.’
High Street firms were last year hit with big rates increases.
Simpson said these businesses will want help announced at the October 28 Budget.
Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the latest review was thus ‘far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off’.

items.body:
Target, the US retail corporation, said it pulled a controversial Halloween costume off its shelves after criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature.
The ad image for the costume, sold as the “Kids’ Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume,” depicted a Black child in a bright orange and black top with solid black gloves and a mask with a wide, toothy smile. Both the child’s pose and the costume’s gloves and mask were likened to caricatures of Black people used in minstrel shows.
“As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry,” Target said in its apology statement. “The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale. We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won’t happen again.”
The costume controversy is just the latest in a series for the Minneapolis-based retailer.
Last year, activists called for a boycott of the company, after its decision to walk-back DEI initiatives. And last week, the American Federation of Teachers, a teachers’ union, called on Target’s CEO, Michael Fiddelke, to call for an end to Operation Metro Surge, Trump’s National Guard push in Minneapolis earlier this year.
Target’s stock price decreased from $137.40 on 24 January, the day the company cut its DEI programs, to $104.70 on 15 March. The company is starting to experience a financial comeback after the initial boycott, but could face other challenges.
